items.label: Grammar explanation

original.title: The German alphabet, special sounds and spelling your name
explanation: German has 26 letters like English, plus ä, ö, ü and ß. The letter names are different, so learn them from the table. You need them to spell your name (buchstabieren), for example on the phone.

Some letters sound different from English. W sounds like English v (Wasser), V often sounds like f (Vater), and Z sounds like ts (Zahl). Ei sounds like English eye (heißen), and ie sounds like ee (Wiedersehen).

Ch, sch and tsch are different sounds. Sch sounds like English sh (Schule). Tsch sounds like English ch in church (Tschüs, Deutsch). Ä, ö and ü are changed vowels called Umlaute, and ß is a long ss sound (heißen).
To greet someone and ask their name, use Hallo, Wie heißt du? and Ich heiße ... To say goodbye, use Tschüs or Auf Wiedersehen.
original.rule_summary: Learn the letter names, spell names letter by letter, and keep tsch (like English ch) apart from sch (like English sh).

original.title: Hello and goodbye in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often greet each other when they enter a small shop, a waiting room or a lift. A short Guten Tag! or Hallo! is polite. Many people use Guten Morgen! in the morning, and Guten Abend! in the evening. With friends and young people, Hallo! and Tschüs! are very common. With adults you do not know, people use Sie and often say Auf Wiedersehen! when they leave. In Switzerland you may hear different greetings, and in southern Germany and Austria people often say Servus or Grüß Gott. You do not need to use these yet, but it is nice to recognise them. Names are often spelled aloud on the phone, so the alphabet is very useful.

intro.title: The German alphabet, special sounds and spelling your name
explanation: German has 26 letters like English, plus ä, ö, ü and ß. The letter names are different, so learn them from the table. You need them to spell your name (buchstabieren), for example on the phone.

Some letters sound different from English. W sounds like English v (Wasser), V often sounds like f (Vater), and Z sounds like ts (Zahl). Ei sounds like English eye (heißen), and ie sounds like ee (Wiedersehen).

Ch, sch and tsch are different sounds. Sch sounds like English sh (Schule). Tsch sounds like English ch in church (Tschüs, Deutsch). Ä, ö and ü are changed vowels called Umlaute, and ß is a sharp s sound, like ss (heißen).
To greet someone and ask their name, use Hallo, Wie heißt du? and Ich heiße ... To say goodbye, use Tschüs or Auf Wiedersehen.

culture.title: Hello and goodbye in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often greet each other when they enter a small shop, a waiting room or a lift. A short Guten Tag! or Hallo! is polite. With adults you do not know, people use Sie and often say Auf Wiedersehen! when they leave. In Switzerland you may hear different greetings, and in southern Germany and Austria people often say Servus or Grüß Gott. You do not need to use these yet, but it is nice to recognise them. Names are often spelled aloud on the phone, so the alphabet is very useful.

original.title: Du or Sie? Introducing yourself
original.note: In German-speaking countries, people choose between du and Sie. You use du with friends, family, children and fellow students. intro.title: Personal pronouns + sein; Ich heiße… / Ich bin… / Ich komme aus…
explanation: Personal pronouns tell us who is speaking or who we are talking about: ich (I), du (you, a friend), er (he), sie (she), es (it), wir (we), ihr (you, several friends), sie (they) and Sie (you, formal). The formal Sie always has a capital S.

original.title: Numbers 0–100, phone numbers and age

From 21 on, German says the small number FIRST: 21 = einundzwanzig, which is literally 'one-and-twenty'. You write it as one long word: ein + und + zwanzig. Note that 1 becomes ein- inside the word. The tens are zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig, hundert.
For a phone number, say each digit one by one: 0151 = null eins fünf eins. Take a short pause between groups. For age, German uses sein, not haben: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt. Ask: Wie alt bist du?

original.title: Phone numbers in German-speaking countries
original.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often say phone numbers in small groups of digits or in pairs, for example "fünf-vier" for 54. Some people say each digit alone. Many people also write the date and the house number after the street name: "Lindenstraße 12". The postcode (Postleitzahl) comes before the city name, for example "10115 Berlin". Germany uses the euro. Switzerland uses its own money, the Swiss franc.

intro.title: Numbers 0–100, phone numbers and age
explanation: Learn 0–12 as separate words: null, eins, zwei, drei, vier, fünf, sechs, sieben, acht, neun, zehn, elf, zwölf. From 13 to 19 you say the small number plus -zehn: dreizehn, vierzehn. Watch the changes: sechzehn (not sechszehn) and siebzehn (not siebenzehn).

From 21 on, German says the small number FIRST: 21 = einundzwanzig, which is literally 'one-and-twenty'. You write it as one long word: ein + und + zwanzig. Note that 1 becomes ein- inside the word. The tens are zwanzig, dreißig, vierzig, fünfzig, sechzig, siebzig, achtzig, neunzig, hundert.
For a phone number, say each digit one by one: 0151 = null eins fünf eins. Take a short pause between groups. For age, German uses sein, not haben: Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt. Ask: Wie alt bist du?
intro.rule_summary: 21–99 = small number + und + ten (einundzwanzig); phone numbers digit by digit; age = Ich bin … Jahre alt.

culture.title: Phone numbers in German-speaking countries
culture.note: In Germany, Austria and Switzerland, people often say phone numbers in small groups of digits or in pairs, for example "vierundfünfzig" for 54. Some people say each digit alone. Zero is "null". When you give a number, people often repeat it to be sure. Mobile numbers are long, so it is normal to say them slowly. If you do not understand, you can say "Noch einmal, bitte." People write the house number after the street name: "Lindenstraße 12". The postcode (Postleitzahl) comes before the city name, for example "10115 Berlin". Germany uses the euro. Switzerland uses its own money, the Swiss franc.
